disclaimer: This is a self-assessment, not an audit. Only an independent CPA firm can issue a SOC 2 report, and this platform has not engaged one. Nothing on this page claims compliance.

frameworks.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
frameworks.note: Subcategory ids and outcomes read from the Core in NIST CSWP 29.
frameworks.license: Work of the U.S. Government (NIST), not subject to copyright in the United States (17 U.S.C. 105).

frameworks.name: CIS Critical Security Controls v8
frameworks.note: Safeguard ids and titles read from CIS's Controls Assessment Specification, one page per Control.

controls.title: Written standards, enforced
controls.asks: The organization writes down what it expects of the people who run the system and holds them to it.
controls.how: A written list of lines the site never crosses is enforced in code: every outbound channel runs the same check before anything is sent, and a test keeps the written list and the code in step.
controls.gap: Nobody signs an acknowledgment of the standards.
controls.solo: The only person bound by the standards is the person who wrote them, so an acknowledgment would be a signature on one's own memo.

mappings.outcome: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities and is communicated and enforced
mappings.why: Written standards that are communicated and enforced are policy that is established and enforced, here conduct standards enforced in code rather than cybersecurity policy alone.

unmapped.reason: CIS Controls v8 has no safeguard on written standards of conduct; its awareness safeguards (Control 14) are about training, not about enforcing a code.

controls.title: Roles, background checks and training
controls.asks: Reporting lines and roles are defined, people with access are screened, and everyone takes security training when hired and every year after.
controls.how: None of this exists in a form an auditor could test. There is one person: no org chart, no hiring process, no training record.
controls.gap: An org chart, a background check, and a dated training record, even for a company of one.
controls.solo: An auditor will still test the one person against these criteria. The fix is paperwork rather than code: a written role, a screening record and an annual training certificate.

mappings.outcome: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices
mappings.why: Roles, screening of people with access, and training at hire are the human resources practices this subcategory names.

mappings.outcome: Personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind
mappings.why: Security training at hire and every year after is awareness and training for personnel.

mappings.outcome: Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood, and enforced
mappings.why: Defined reporting lines and roles are the established and communicated roles this subcategory covers, which also asks for authorities and enforcement.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness Program
mappings.why: An annual training record is evidence of a security awareness program; the criterion also covers roles and screening, which CIS does not address.

controls.title: A current description of the system
controls.asks: The organization knows and documents what the system is, where its boundaries are, and who can reach what.
controls.how: A written threat model names every kind of actor, what each can reach and what bounds it. A public system map shows the parts and how they connect.
controls.gap: The threat model was last verified on July 4, 2026. Nothing schedules the next review.
evidence: docs/capabilities/08-security-privacy-resilience.md#Threat model - actors and what they can reach

mappings.outcome: Representations of the organization's authorized network communication and internal and external network data flows are maintained
mappings.why: A system map showing parts and connections is a representation of data flows, though the criterion also covers boundaries and who can reach what.

mappings.outcome: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
mappings.why: Documenting what the system is covers an inventory of the software, services and systems in it.

mappings.outcome: Internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded
mappings.why: A written threat model naming each kind of actor is a record of internal and external threats.

mappings.outcome: Conduct Threat Modeling
mappings.why: A threat model that names actors, what each can reach and what bounds it is the threat modeling this safeguard asks for.

mappings.outcome: Document Data Flows
mappings.why: A system map showing how parts connect documents data flows, though this safeguard is specific to data and the map is not.

controls.title: Telling users what is happening
controls.asks: Users are told about the system's commitments and about incidents that affect them.
controls.how: A public status page reports each component as up, degraded or down, from a health check every three hours, and a privacy page lists what the site stores in a visitor's browser.

mappings.outcome: Critical objectives, capabilities, and services that external stakeholders depend on or expect from the organization are understood and communicated
mappings.why: A status page tells users what the services they depend on are doing, which is communicating those services' state; the subcategory is about the objectives and capabilities themselves.

mappings.outcome: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents
mappings.why: Telling users about incidents that affect them is notifying external stakeholders of incidents.

mappings.outcome: Define Mechanisms for Communicating During Incident Response
mappings.why: A public status page is one mechanism for communicating during an incident, though this safeguard names internal and external channels generally.

controls.title: A risk assessment that repeats
controls.asks: Risks to the system are identified and analyzed, and the assessment is repeated as things change.
controls.how: The threat model names its known gaps instead of hiding them, and the one path that merges code without a person has its remaining risk written down and accepted.
controls.gap: The assessment was written once. There is no second one to show that it repeats, and no calendar that makes it.
evidence: docs/capabilities/08-security-privacy-resilience.md#Named here as the gap rather than

mappings.outcome: Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization
mappings.why: Identifying and analyzing risks to the system uses threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods and impacts to prioritize responses.

mappings.outcome: A standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing, and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated
mappings.why: Repeating the assessment as things change needs a standard method to calculate, document and prioritize risk, which the criterion implies.

mappings.outcome: Conduct Threat Modeling
mappings.why: CIS has no enterprise risk assessment safeguard; threat modeling is its nearest application-level analog of identifying and analyzing risk.

controls.title: Checking that the controls still work
controls.asks: The organization evaluates whether its controls are present and functioning, and acts on what it finds.
controls.how: Every scheduled job is listed in a catalog that a test keeps in step with the real schedules, and a dashboard sorts each job into fired, failing or silent.
controls.gap: The scheduled jobs were all switched off from July 29 to October 8, 2026 to cut the monthly bill, so the dashboard has a gap in its record for that period. They run again now, but a few stay off on purpose.
evidence: docs/ops/CRON-FREEZE.md#Every scheduled GitHub Actions workflow is paused

mappings.outcome: Organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed
mappings.why: Evaluating whether controls still function and acting on what is found is evaluating and reviewing risk management performance.

mappings.outcome: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored to find potentially adverse events
mappings.why: A dashboard sorting each scheduled job into fired, failing or silent monitors software and runtime for adverse events, a narrower sense of the criterion.

mappings.outcome: Validate Security Measures
mappings.why: Checking that deployed controls still work is validating security measures, though this safeguard sits in a penetration testing Control.

controls.title: Policies deployed as tests
controls.asks: Control activities are put in place through technology and through written policies that people follow.
controls.how: Policies here are tests that run on every change: the credential inventory, rate-limit coverage, the boundary around client records, the lines the site never crosses. The build fails if any one of them breaks.

mappings.outcome: Secure software development practices are integrated, and their performance is monitored throughout the software development life cycle
mappings.why: Policies deployed as tests on every change are secure development practices integrated into the software life cycle.

mappings.outcome: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities and is communicated and enforced
mappings.why: A test that fails the build when a policy breaks is how that policy is enforced, not only communicated.

mappings.outcome: Implement Code-Level Security Checks
mappings.why: Tests on every change that check credentials, route protection and data boundaries are code-level security checks.

controls.title: Least-privilege access
controls.asks: Access to information and systems is limited to what each person or process needs.
controls.how: Access is an ordered ladder: none, view, edit, admin. A member of a shared board sees only that board, and an unknown board and a board you are not on both answer "not found". Automated agents act only through tokens scoped to a grant.

mappings.outcome: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
mappings.why: An ordered ladder of access levels with scoped tokens is permissions defined by policy and enforced on least privilege.

mappings.outcome: Define and Maintain Role-Based Access Control
mappings.why: Ordered access levels and board-scoped membership are role-based access control defined and maintained.

mappings.outcome: Configure Data Access Control Lists
mappings.why: Scoping each shared board to its members is a data access control list, here applied to application records.

controls.title: Reviewing who has access
controls.asks: Access is granted through a process, removed when it is no longer needed, and reviewed on a schedule.
controls.how: Grants are recorded, and every use of an agent's access token is written to an audit log. But nobody reviews the full list of who can reach what on a schedule.
controls.gap: A dated, recurring access review with a record of what was removed.
controls.solo: The reviewer and the person whose access is being reviewed would be the same person.

mappings.outcome: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
mappings.why: The criterion's missing piece, a scheduled review of who can reach what, is the reviewed part of this subcategory.

mappings.outcome: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
mappings.why: Granting, removing and reviewing access is managing identities and credentials for people, services and hardware.

mappings.outcome: Establish an Access Granting Process
mappings.why: Recording grants is the access granting process this safeguard asks for.

mappings.outcome: Establish an Access Revoking Process
mappings.why: Removing access that is no longer needed is the access revoking process this safeguard asks for.

mappings.outcome: Disable Dormant Accounts
mappings.why: A scheduled review of who has access is how dormant accounts are found and disabled.

controls.title: Credentials encrypted and accounted for
controls.asks: Credentials that protect the system are themselves protected.
controls.how: Stored credentials are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, changed from an admin screen without a redeploy, and every change is logged. A test fails when code uses a credential the ledger has never heard of.
controls.gap: Keys are rotated when someone decides to, not on a calendar.

mappings.outcome: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization
mappings.why: Encrypted stored credentials, rotated from one screen with a change log, are credentials for services managed by the organization.

mappings.outcome: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
mappings.why: Encrypting stored credentials protects data at rest, for the credential store only.

mappings.outcome: Encrypt Sensitive Data At Rest
mappings.why: Encrypting stored credentials with AES-256-GCM is encrypting sensitive data at rest, for the credential store only.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Accounts
mappings.why: A ledger of every outside service the site holds a key for resembles an inventory of service accounts, though the ledger lists credentials rather than accounts.

controls.title: Protecting the edges
controls.asks: The system is protected against threats from outside its boundaries.
controls.how: Every route that writes data must be rate-limited, gated behind sign-in, verified by a signature, or listed with a written reason. A test fails on any new route that is none of these. Inbound webhooks are checked with a constant-time comparison.
controls.gap: The rate limiter keeps a separate count on each server instance, so a caller spread across instances gets more than the limit. The security doc says so.

mappings.outcome: Networks and environments are protected from unauthorized logical access and usage
mappings.why: Rate limits, sign-in gates and signature checks protect the system from unauthorized use across its network boundary.

mappings.outcome: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
mappings.why: Verifying inbound webhooks with a constant-time signature comparison is verifying identity assertions.

mappings.outcome: Apply Secure Design Principles in Application Architectures
mappings.why: Requiring every writing route to be gated, rate-limited or signature-verified is a secure design principle applied to the application architecture.

controls.title: Encryption in transit
controls.asks: Information moving between the system and its users is protected.
controls.how: Every response tells browsers to use HTTPS only, for two years, subdomains included.
controls.gap: There is no full Content Security Policy. The config explains why one was not added blind.

mappings.outcome: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-transit are protected
mappings.why: An HTTPS-only response header protects data in transit, as one mechanism rather than a full account of every path.

mappings.outcome: Encrypt Sensitive Data in Transit
mappings.why: An HTTPS-only response header is encrypting sensitive data in transit for browsers, as one mechanism.

controls.title: Finding vulnerabilities
controls.asks: The organization detects new vulnerabilities and unauthorized or malicious software.
controls.how: Nothing scans for them. No automated dependency updates or vulnerability scans are configured, and the install step in CI skips npm's own audit.
controls.gap: A dependency scanner on every pull request, and a record of what was found and fixed.

mappings.outcome: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
mappings.why: Detecting new vulnerabilities in assets is identifying, validating and recording them.

mappings.outcome: Software is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk
mappings.why: Dependency updates are software maintained commensurate with risk, the remediation side of the criterion.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain a Vulnerability Management Process
mappings.why: Detecting and handling new vulnerabilities is the vulnerability management process this safeguard asks for.

mappings.outcome: Perform Automated Vulnerability Scans of Internal Enterprise Assets
mappings.why: Automated scans are the mechanism the criterion names; this safeguard is written for internal assets and a hosted web application is an adaptation.

mappings.outcome: Use Up-to-Date and Trusted Third-Party Software Components
mappings.why: Dependency updates are use of up-to-date and trusted third-party software components.

controls.title: Noticing when something breaks
controls.asks: The system is monitored for anomalies that could mean an attack, an error or an outage.
controls.how: Errors go through one reporting function. A watcher compares the live deployment with the latest commit and alerts when production stalls, and it runs off the hosting provider so it still fires during that provider's outage.
controls.gap: Both watchers run on schedule, but the health check looks every three hours and the deploy watcher twice a day, so an outage can go unheard for hours. Every alert reaches one person, and nobody else is watching when that person is away.

mappings.outcome: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored to find potentially adverse events
mappings.why: Error reporting and a watcher comparing the live deployment with the latest commit monitor software and runtime for adverse events.

mappings.outcome: Information on adverse events is provided to authorized staff and tools
mappings.why: Alerts that reach the operator are information on adverse events provided to authorized staff.

mappings.outcome: Centralize Security Event Alerting
mappings.why: Alerts routed to one operator are security event alerting centralized, at the scale of one person.

controls.title: Responding to incidents
controls.asks: Incidents are evaluated and contained, then fixed, and the lessons are written down.
controls.how: A failed check opens an incident, which moves through one state machine until it is resolved, and alerts page the operator by Telegram.
controls.gap: There is no written response plan and no postmortem convention. The security doc names the missing convention as a gap.

mappings.outcome: Incidents are declared when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria
mappings.why: A failed check that opens an incident is declaring an incident when an adverse event meets defined criteria.

mappings.outcome: The incident response plan is executed in coordination with relevant third parties once an incident is declared
mappings.why: A state machine that carries an incident to resolution is executing an incident response plan, without third-party coordination.

mappings.outcome: Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident
mappings.why: Writing down the lessons from an incident includes establishing what happened and the root cause.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain an Incident Response Process
mappings.why: A single state machine from detection to resolution is an incident response process, though the criterion adds containment and lessons.

mappings.outcome: Conduct Post-Incident Reviews
mappings.why: The criterion's final step, writing down the lessons, is the post-incident review this safeguard asks for.

controls.title: Every change tested and approved
controls.asks: Changes to the system are authorized and designed, then tested and approved, with a record kept, before they reach production.
controls.how: Every change lands through a pull request that must pass lint, the full test suite and a build that matches production. One narrow path merges small agent-written fixes without a person, and it fails closed.
controls.gap: Nobody but the author approves a change. The one automated reviewer was switched off when its API budget went to zero.
controls.solo: Separation of duties needs a second person: whoever writes a change should not be the one who approves it.

mappings.outcome: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked
mappings.why: Changes authorized, tested, approved and recorded before production are changes managed, assessed for risk and tracked.

mappings.outcome: Configuration management practices are established and applied
mappings.why: A pull request gated by lint, tests and a production-matching build is part of how configuration is managed and applied.

mappings.outcome: Secure software development practices are integrated, and their performance is monitored throughout the software development life cycle
mappings.why: Required lint, test and build checks on every change are secure development practices integrated into the life cycle.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain a Secure Application Development Process
mappings.why: A required pull request path with checks is a secure application development process, though v8 has no change management safeguard as such.

mappings.outcome: Implement Code-Level Security Checks
mappings.why: Lint and the full test suite on every change are code-level checks.

controls.title: Vendor risk
controls.asks: Risks from vendors and business partners are assessed and managed.
controls.how: The credential ledger names every outside service the site holds a key for, so the vendor list is complete and a test keeps it that way.
controls.gap: Nobody collects the vendors' own SOC 2 reports or writes down a review of them.

mappings.outcome: Inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained
mappings.why: A ledger of every outside service the site holds a key for is an inventory of services provided by suppliers.

mappings.outcome: The risks posed by a supplier, their products and services, and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship
mappings.why: Recording every vendor is the first step of understanding and monitoring the risk each poses, which the ledger alone does not do.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Providers
mappings.why: A complete, test-held vendor list is an inventory of service providers.

controls.title: Backups that restore
controls.asks: Data is backed up, and recovery is tested.
controls.how: A weekly job dumps the business-critical tables, encrypts the archive, copies it offsite, then restores it into a scratch database and checks the rows, because a backup that cannot restore is not a backup. A runbook sets recovery targets for each zone. Portfolio OS, the business record, has its own nightly encrypted export and restore test, and records each result.
controls.gap: The job was paused from July 29 to October 8, 2026. Since the schedule came back, every weekly restore test has passed, six in a row from October 11 to November 15. A Type II period is usually three months or more, so the record is real but still short.

mappings.outcome: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested
mappings.why: Weekly encrypted, offsite, restore-tested backups are backups created, protected, maintained and tested.

mappings.outcome: The integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration
mappings.why: Restoring into a scratch database and checking the rows verifies backup integrity before real use.

mappings.outcome: Perform Automated Backups
mappings.why: A scheduled weekly dump of the critical tables is automated backups.

mappings.outcome: Protect Recovery Data
mappings.why: Encrypting the archive and copying it offsite is protecting recovery data.

mappings.outcome: Test Data Recovery
mappings.why: Restoring into a scratch database and checking the rows is testing data recovery.

mappings.outcome: Establish and Maintain a Data Recovery Process
mappings.why: A runbook with recovery targets for each zone is a data recovery process.

controls.title: Capacity and cost limits
controls.asks: Capacity is managed so the system can meet its commitments.
controls.how: AI spend is logged on every call, and a brake stops paid calls at the monthly ceiling before a runaway bill can take the service down. Public endpoints are rate-limited.

mappings.outcome: Adequate resource capacity to ensure availability is maintained
mappings.why: Rate limits and a spend brake keep demand within what the service can carry, though the subcategory is about capacity itself.

unmapped.reason: CIS Controls v8 has no safeguard on capacity planning or cost limits; its availability coverage is backup and recovery (Control 11).

controls.title: Confidential records walled off
controls.asks: Confidential information is identified and protected.
controls.how: A client's records can be imported only by that client's own module. A test scans the codebase and fails if anything else reaches in, and it also fails if it scanned too few files to mean anything.

mappings.outcome: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties
mappings.why: Letting only a client's own module import that client's records enforces access by role on the most sensitive data.

mappings.outcome: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained
mappings.why: Naming which records are confidential and walling them off starts an inventory of designated data types, without the metadata.

mappings.outcome: Configure Data Access Control Lists
mappings.why: A code-level wall around a client's records is an access control list on that data, enforced by test rather than by a file system.

mappings.outcome: Segment Data Processing and Storage Based on Sensitivity
mappings.why: A test-held wall that isolates one client's records from the rest is segmenting data handling by sensitivity.

controls.title: Disposal on a schedule
controls.asks: Confidential information is disposed of when it is no longer needed.
controls.how: A written retention policy deletes dinner-guest replies 30 days after the event and retires stale scraped listings, and unclaimed anonymous boards are deleted after 30 days.
controls.gap: The mail inbox declares a retention period it does not enforce. The deletion sweeps run again as of October 8, 2026 after a pause since July 29.

mappings.outcome: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles
mappings.why: Deleting records after a retention period is managing data through to the end of its life cycle.

mappings.outcome: Enforce Data Retention
mappings.why: A written retention policy with scheduled deletes is data retention enforced.

mappings.outcome: Securely Dispose of Data
mappings.why: Deleting records after a period is disposal, though the safeguard also covers how thoroughly data is destroyed.

controls.title: Accurate processing
controls.asks: Inputs and processing are complete and accurate.
controls.how: Money is stored as whole cents, never as floating-point dollars. Published figures are recomputed on every change. Payment webhooks are accepted only with a valid signature.

mappings.outcome: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified
mappings.why: Accepting payment webhooks only with a valid signature is verifying identity assertions, one input-integrity check among the criterion's several.

unmapped.reason: Processing integrity (whole-cent money, recomputed figures) is an application correctness concern; CIS v8 has no safeguard on it, and 16.12 code-level checks was considered and rejected as too loose a fit.

controls.title: Notice and choice
controls.asks: People are told what personal information is collected and are given choices about it.
controls.how: A privacy page lists every cookie the site sets. The one optional analytics cookie stays off unless the visitor accepts it.
controls.gap: The notice covers the browser. It does not describe the personal information held in the private household and client tools.

mappings.outcome: Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements regarding cybersecurity - including privacy and civil liberties obligations - are understood and managed
mappings.why: A privacy notice and an opt-in analytics cookie respond to privacy obligations; the subcategory is about understanding and managing those obligations.

unmapped.reason: CIS Controls v8 is a security framework with no safeguard on privacy notices or consent; its data safeguards (Control 3) concern protection and handling.
